## Overview

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News-category piece (578 words, within the 400-1200 range) using the site's standard Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Analysis format. Prose is clear, neutral, and consistently attributes each claim to a named outlet. The closing Analysis paragraph is clearly independent editorial commentary (four-month detection-to-notification gap, insurance-sector breach pattern) rather than a sourced claim, which is appropriate for this section.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 6 source snapshots were read in full from the gzipped HTML files in sources/2026-07/assuranceamerica-data-breach-exposes-drivers-license-records-of-nearly-7-million-people/ (source-0 through source-5). Manifest confirms all 6 fetched with status 200 (2 via Archive.org fallback: BleepingComputer and eSecurity Planet, both because the live URL bot-blocked the fetcher despite returning 200). SHA-256 of each decompressed file was independently recomputed and matches the manifest exactly for all 6 snapshots, confirming snapshot integrity. (1) source-0 BleepingComputer confirms the March 17/16 detection timeline, the 9,500-agent/14-state footprint, and the exact 6,998,886-person figure (via a Maine AG filing). (2) source-1 eSecurity Planet confirms the same footprint and figure (via the same Maine AG filing) and the full post-incident response list (disabled credentials, terminated sessions, isolated systems, notified law enforcement, reset passwords, enhanced monitoring, employee training) verbatim as itemized in the article. (3) source-2 CyberInsider confirms the 'Atlanta-based' and 'founded in 1998' facts, the 'largest known exposure of driver's license data this year' framing, the March 17 detection date, the June 15 investigation-conclusion date, and the exact data-element list (names, contact info, auto insurance policy/account info, driver and vehicle info, claims info, driver's license numbers) attributed to the notification letter. (4) source-3 TechCrunch confirms the March 17 discovery date, the June 15 investigation conclusion, the verbatim quotes 'discovered hackers in its computer systems on March 17,' 'targeted one of the Company's employees,' 'disabled compromised credentials,' and the stolen-data-categories quote about 'customers' auto insurance policies and accounts, their drivers and vehicles, and details about customer claims' — all verified word-for-word against the snapshot. It also confirms the Indiana AG filing detail (6.99 million people, July 10 notification date) and the unanswered-questions-to-CEO-Skruck-and-founder-Millner detail. (5) source-4 SC Media (scworld.com) confirms the 'largest known exposure' framing and the employee-targeted-credential-compromise claim without further technical detail, matching the article's characterization. (6) source-5 Malwarebytes confirms the no-attribution-to-a-specific-threat-group/no-reported-ransom-demand claim and the same core timeline/figures. No snapshot was fetched via live WebFetch; all verification was performed against the committed gzip snapshots per the mandatory process.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every direct quotation in the article (four total, all from TechCrunch) was checked against the source-3 snapshot and found verbatim. The 6,998,886-person figure, the March 17/16 timeline, the June 15 investigation-close date, the 9,500-agent/14-state footprint, the 'founded in 1998' and 'Atlanta-based' facts, and the full data-element and remediation-step lists all check out precisely against their cited (or, for two descriptive clauses, another cited-elsewhere) source. No fabricated statistics, no invented quotes, no fake citations.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout. No sensationalism, loaded language, or editorializing; the 'largest known exposure... so far in 2026' framing is itself attributed to two of the cited outlets rather than asserted independently.
editor_notes.originality: Searched src/content/articles/2026-07/ (and confirmed via grep across the full articles tree) for prior AssuranceAmerica coverage — none exists. This is a genuinely new topic, distinct from other 2026-07 cybersecurity/data-breach articles already published (e.g. the Mastra npm supply-chain and CISA SharePoint RCE pieces cover unrelated incidents).
concerns: Allowlist gap only, not a content-accuracy issue: esecurityplanet.com is not yet in config/source_allowlist.txt, which is what drove the automated script's APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS suggestion. Manually verified eSecurity Planet as a legitimate, editorially-staffed cybersecurity trade publication (part of the TechnologyAdvice network, named byline with stated credentials, editorial-independence disclosure) whose cited content fully supports the claims attributed to it. This does not warrant a reader-facing correction (there is no factual error to disclose); recommend a separate maintenance PR add the domain to the allowlist.

Minor attribution-of-phrasing issue (not a fact error): the Overview's opening sentence ('AssuranceAmerica is notifying nearly 7 million people that hackers stole sensitive customer information, including driver's license numbers, following a cyberattack discovered in March') is reproduced near-verbatim from CyberInsider's own lead sentence but is cited to TechCrunch. The underlying facts are independently and accurately confirmed by the TechCrunch snapshot itself, so no reader is misled about substance — only the specific prose happens to originate with a different (also cited, also verified) outlet. Two further sentences (the Indiana AG filing sentence and the TechCrunch-questions-unanswered sentence) reproduce TechCrunch's own phrasing almost word-for-word without quotation marks, though correctly attributed to TechCrunch. None of this rises to fabrication or misattribution of fact, but it falls short of the outlet's own house style of paraphrasing outside quotes; noted as a craft recommendation rather than a correction.
recommendations: Add esecurityplanet.com to config/source_allowlist.txt in a maintenance PR — verified as a legitimate, reputable cybersecurity trade outlet.
Coach the contributor bot to either quote verbatim source phrasing with quotation marks or rewrite it in its own words, rather than reproducing another outlet's original sentence structure unquoted.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Substantively accurate, well-sourced News piece on a genuinely new topic. Every specific figure, date, and direct quotation is corroborated verbatim across multiple independently fetched sources, and no fabricated or misattributed facts were found. The sole automated finding (esecurityplanet.com missing from the source allowlist) is a housekeeping gap, not a content defect — the outlet was manually verified as legitimate and its cited content is accurate. A secondary style observation (some non-quoted sentences closely mirror source phrasing) does not affect factual accuracy and does not warrant a public correction. APPROVE.
